extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; editors and writers of periodical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical remarks for composing and evaluating early-18th-century periodical/moral essays in the manner of Addison and Steele: what qualities, tones, and methods made the Spectator effective. Useful for essayists, editors, and literary students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship and collaborative editorial shaping
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor/colleague can extract and encourage excellent productions from another writer ('I claim to myself the merit of having extorted excellent productions...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial work is a creative, shaping force — unselfish collaboration (the 'whetstone' role) can improve and enable a writer's best work; credit and mutual support between collaborators matter to the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious earnestness as a foundational moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The deep foundations of the Spectator 'were laid in the religious earnestness that was alike in both' authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sincere moral/religious purpose underpins persuasive periodical writing; seriousness of purpose lends authority and cohesion to essays, even when combined with humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a broad public rather than only for elite patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spoke for the people and looked to the people for approval and support' — the Spectator addressed popular influence rather than merely flattering cultivated patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity, accessibility, and public-minded topics; avoid writing that exclusively targets a narrow, highly cultivated audience if the aim is broad influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural thought and speech (Saxon strength) over affected French/Latin polish
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Finding this to be not Latin but Saxon, they would have sought to give it strength and harmony' — a recommendation to base English prose on native idiom rather than imported Latinate/French affectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain, strong English idiom for force and harmony; avoid undue reliance on fashionable foreignisms that obscure natural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical models judiciously, not with blind obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: While classical authorities (Virgil, Horace, Aristotle) are valuable, blind submission to French/Latinate critical law is discouraged; apply classical rules' spirit rather than their letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from ancient models to gain discipline and proportion, but adapt rules to English strengths and contemporary purposes (e.g., justification of Milton by classical measure rather than slavish imitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wit and humour with humanity and earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: The best writing combines 'sportive humour, delicately whimsical and gaily wise' with sympathetic, moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let wit enliven essays but temper it with genuine human sympathy and moral seriousness so humour does not become mere ornament or cynicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage sympathy with real life and social realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's sympathies 'were with all England' and he addressed 'actual wrongs, actual remedies' — effective essays attend to the concrete conditions and sufferings of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground commentary in observed social realities and practical concerns; moralizing abstractly is weaker than addressing particular human situations and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive didacticism and airs of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's 'Christian Hero' was judged 'too didactic'; an air of superiority is 'repugnant' to the writer's nature and to good persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer demonstration, character, and narrative to blunt preaching; preserve modesty of tone and allow readers to be persuaded rather than lectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, restraint and propriety in tone (temper strong impulses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison 'bridled' his muse and used classical restraint; avoid uncontrolled boldness or extravagant 'formal raptures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrain rhetorical excesses; aim for measured expression that balances feeling and form, especially when dealing with elevated subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine analytical reflection with practical convivial sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison is described as 'speculative' and analytical; Steele as 'practical' and sympathetic — together they show the value of both tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective periodical essays often blend thoughtful analysis with practical sensibility and conversational warmth; use both critique and human example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value imagination but temper its 'wildness' with taste
rubrics_metrics.description: On imagination: Addison 'but half escapes from the conventions of his time' — imaginative passages should be employed thoughtfully given contemporary taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative description to enrich essays, but be mindful of audience taste and avoid alienating readers with unchecked flights of fancy; reconcile imagination with critical good sense.
